prompt:
Write a technical description of about 1,000 words of what happens between a browser being given an HTTPS address and the first byte of the response arriving. The reader is a junior web developer.

Do not use em dashes.

text:
From HTTPS Address to First Byte: What the Browser Does

When you type https://www.example.com/products into a browser and press Enter, a surprising amount of work happens before the first byte of the response arrives. The delay you perceive as "waiting" is a chain of separate steps, each with its own cost. Knowing them helps you understand performance advice such as "reduce redirects" or "use a CDN".

1. Parsing the URL

The browser first splits the address into parts. The scheme is https, the host is www.example.com, the port is implied (443 for HTTPS), and the path is /products. The scheme tells the browser to use an encrypted connection. Before going to the network, the browser also checks a few local rules. It may consult its HSTS list (HTTP Strict Transport Security), which records sites that must only be reached over HTTPS. If you typed http:// for such a site, the browser upgrades it internally without sending any request.

2. Checking caches and service workers

Next the browser asks whether it needs the network at all. If a service worker controls this origin, it runs first and may answer from its own cache. Otherwise the browser checks its HTTP cache. A fresh cached copy, one whose Cache-Control or Expires headers say it is still valid, is used immediately and nothing is sent. A stale copy may be revalidated later with a conditional request. If nothing usable exists, the work continues.

3. DNS resolution

Networks route traffic by IP address, not by name, so the browser must turn www.example.com into an address such as 93.184.216.34. It checks several places in order: its own DNS cache, the operating system's cache and hosts file, and then a recursive resolver, usually run by your ISP or a public provider. If the resolver has no cached answer, it walks the hierarchy. It asks a root server which servers handle .com, asks those which servers handle example.com, and finally asks the authoritative server for the record. The answer carries a TTL (time to live) that says how long it may be cached. A cold lookup can take tens of milliseconds or more, while a cached one is nearly instant. Modern browsers may also request HTTPS or SVCB records that advertise HTTP/3 support, and some use encrypted DNS (DNS over HTTPS) so the lookup cannot be read in transit.

4. Opening a TCP connection

With an IP address, the browser opens a connection. For HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 this means TCP, which begins with a three-way handshake. The browser sends SYN, the server replies SYN-ACK, and the browser sends ACK. This costs one full round trip, meaning the time for a packet to travel to the server and back. If the server is on another continent, a round trip may be 100 to 200 milliseconds, and this is why geographic distance matters so much. HTTP/3 avoids TCP entirely and runs over QUIC on UDP, which merges the transport and security handshakes and saves a round trip.

5. The TLS handshake

Because the scheme is HTTPS, the browser must now set up encryption on top of the connection. With TLS 1.3 the exchange is roughly this:

- The browser sends a ClientHello listing the TLS versions and cipher suites it supports, a random value, a key share for key exchange, and the Server Name Indication (SNI), which tells the server which hostname you want. This matters because one IP address often hosts many sites.
- The server replies with a ServerHello choosing the parameters, its own key share, and its certificate.
- Both sides combine the key shares to derive the same session keys, without ever sending the keys themselves. Everything after this point is encrypted.

The certificate is how the browser decides whether the server is really who it claims to be. The browser verifies that the certificate was signed by a certificate authority it trusts, that the chain of signatures is intact, that the certificate has not expired, and that its names include www.example.com. It may also check revocation status. If any check fails, you see the full-page security warning rather than the site.

TLS 1.3 needs one round trip for this handshake. Older TLS 1.2 needed two. If the browser has connected before, session resumption can shorten this further, and 0-RTT mode lets a client send data in its very first flight, with some replay-attack caveats. Also note that when a connection to the same host is already open, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 let the browser reuse it, skipping steps 3 to 5 completely. This is one reason loading many resources from a single origin is cheap.

During the handshake the browser also negotiates the application protocol using ALPN. This is where the server and browser agree to speak HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1 over the encrypted channel, without costing an extra round trip.

6. Sending the HTTP request

Now the browser sends the actual request through the encrypted channel. In HTTP/1.1 syntax it looks like this:

GET /products HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Accept: text/html
Accept-Encoding: gzip, br
Cookie: session=abc123

In HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 the same information is carried in compressed binary frames, but the meaning is identical: a method, a path, and headers. The browser attaches relevant cookies for this site, advertises which compression formats it understands, and includes caching headers if it is revalidating a stale copy. There is no body for a simple GET.

7. Server-side work and the wait

The request travels to the server, often not directly to your application but first to a CDN edge, load balancer, or reverse proxy. A CDN may answer straight from its cache. If not, the request is forwarded to an origin server, where your application routes it, runs middleware such as authentication, queries databases, renders a template or builds JSON, and produces a response. All of this time is called server think time, and it is the part you control most directly as a developer.

8. The first byte

When the server sends the first bytes of the response, the status line and headers, the browser receives them. The time from starting the navigation to this moment is called Time to First Byte (TTFB). It is the sum of everything above: redirects, DNS, TCP, TLS, the request travelling there, server processing, and the first bytes travelling back.

You can inspect these phases yourself. In the browser's DevTools Network panel, select a request and open the Timing tab. It breaks the request into stalled, DNS lookup, initial connection, SSL, request sent, waiting (TTFB), and content download. The curl command shows similar detail with curl -w and its timing variables.

Practical takeaways

- Avoid unnecessary redirects. Each one repeats much of this process, and http to https redirects can be avoided with HSTS.
- Use a CDN to put servers physically closer to users, which shrinks every round trip.
- Keep connections alive and reuse them. HTTP/2 multiplexing and keep-alive remove repeated handshakes.
- Cache aggressively with correct Cache-Control headers so many requests never reach the network.
- Optimize server work. Slow queries and uncached rendering show up directly as waiting time.
- Use preconnect and dns-prefetch hints for origins you know the page will need soon.

The key idea is that "the request" is really a sequence of small negotiations, and most of the delay comes from round trips rather than from bandwidth. Reducing round trips, by caching, reusing connections, and moving content closer to users, is usually the most effective way to speed up that first byte.
